Enhancing methanogenesis efficiency in anaerobic digestion of food waste 
through incremental salinity and nanobubble utilization to domesticate 
inoculum: Adaptability and optimal inoculation ratios
Tingting Hou a,b, Youzhou Jiao a,c, Jiamin Zhao d, Zhenya Zhang e, Zhongfang Lei e,  
Guizhuan Xu a,b, Xiaohui Pan a,b, Pengfei Li a,b, Francesco Petracchini f, Chao He a,b,*
a Key Laboratory of New Materials and Facilities for Rural Renewable Energy of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, College of Mechanical & Electrical Engineering, 
Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou, 450002, China
b Henan International Joint Laboratory of Biomass Energy and Nanomaterials, Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou, 450002, Henan, China
c Henan University of Engineering, Zhengzhou, 451191, China
d National Science Library, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
e Faculty of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki, 305-8572, Japan
f National Research Council of Italy- Institute of Atmospheric Pollution Research, 29300, Rome, Italy
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Food waste
Salinity tolerance
Methane yield enhancement
Air nanobubble water
A B S T R A C T
High salinity inhibits methane production in food waste (FW) anaerobic digestion (AD). This study investigated 
the salinity tolerance (1 %–3 %) of inoculum acclimated with air nanobubble water (Air-NBW) and evaluated 
methanogenic potential under 3 % salinity across varying inoculum-to-substrate (I/S) ratios (volatile solids (VS) 
basis). As results, the methane yield of the Air-NBW group significantly increased by 31 %, 18 %, and 16 % (p <
0.05 for all phases) relative to the control group across the three phases. Remarkably, the lag period in the Air- 
NBW group exhibited a notable reduction as the salinity increased, particularly at the salinity of 2 % where a 
significant decrease of 14 days in the lag period was observed in comparison to the control group. Additionally, 
the Air-NBW digester showed a non-significant increase in methane yield (228.88 ± 4.36 mL/g-VSfed, p = 0.061) 
at I/S = 1, while demonstrating a significant increase to 307.45 ± 3.77 mL/g-VSfed at I/S = 0.5 (p = 0.007 <
0.05) compared to the DW groups at equivalent I/S ratios. These results indicate that the using a salinity- 
adaptable inoculum could effectively facilitate the swift initiation and sustained stability of FW digesters.
1. Introduction
The rapid growth of the catering business has generated considerable 
Food waste (FW) that should be urgently disposed of in an effective 
manner. Recently, FW has been confirmed as one of the preferred sub­
strates for anaerobic digestion (AD) for energy recovery since it covers 
high levels of biodegradables (e.g., polysaccharides, proteins, and oils) 
[1]. However, several environmental factors have frequently hindered 
the AD of FW. For instance, high salinity in FW, a common challenge, is 
primarily attributed to the extensive use of sodium chloride-based salt 
(typically > 97 % in China) as a cooking seasoning [2].
For the AD system, Na+ exerts more significant inhibiting effects 
than Cl−[3]. A specific limit of Na+ concentration is favorable for the 
metabolic activity of microorganisms (e.g., facilitating the synthesis of 
adenosine triphosphate, or stimulating the oxidation of nitramine 
adenine dinucleotides) [4,5]. Conversely, high Na+ concentration will 
be toxic to microbial metabolism to a certain extent. When external 
osmotic pressure exceeds intracellular pressure, water flows out, causing 
cellular protoplasm separation, leading to cell lysis and death [6]. Also, 
high salinity is likely to result in lower dehydrogenase activity, serving 
as a vital indicator of microbial activity in the AD digesters [7]. Existing 
research has confirmed that a variety of salinity levels produced varying 
inhibition degrees of CH4 yield in the AD of FW digesters, with higher 
inhibition levels with the increase of the salt levels. For instance, the 
inhibition degrees of CH4 yield in the one-phase AD of kitchen waste 
system with 10–16 g NaCl/L range from 24 % to 81 % [8]. Zhang et al. 
[9] suggested that high salinity (>15 g/L)) would reduce the diversity 
and the abundance of methanogens. Besides, NaCl concentration also

affects the biogas composition from kitchen waste AD, with methane 
content decreasing as NaCl concentration increases [10]. Therefore, 
relieving the inhibition of high salinity is essential to improve methane 
production from AD of FW.
The existing common strategy refers to the reduction of the salinity 
in the AD of the FW system by co-digestion with other low-salt substrates 
or by using water and wastewater to dilute the salinity of the AD system. 
A further strategy is to resist the adverse high-salt environment by 
improving microbial activity and salt tolerance of microorganisms. 
External osmoprotectants (e.g., betaine, trehalose, and amino acids) can 
effectively restore the activity of methanogens under high-salt condi­
tions [11]. Additionally, existing research has confirmed that undo­
mesticated anaerobic microorganisms took nearly 20 d to adapt to 
high-salt environments [12]. In contrast, anaerobic microorganisms that 
have been acclimated to salt could effectively counteract the inhibitory 
influences of certain salinity levels on methanogenesis [13]. As indi­
cated by the Zhang et al. [10], although methane production, dehy­
drogenase, and coenzyme F420 activities were first enhanced and then 
decreased with increasing salt concentration, the methanogenic bacteria 
(Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina) exhibited potential adaptability to 
high-salt environments after domestication.
Nanobubble water (NBW) refers to water containing nanobubbles 
smaller than 1 μm in diameter, noted for its pollution-free nature, high 
stability, superior gas solubility, and negative zeta potential. Previous 
research has confirmed that NBW possesses the remarkable ability to 
significantly increase microbial activity [12,14,15]. Hence, the intro­
duction of NBW into AD systems has emerged as a novel strategy, proven 
to boost the bioactivities of enzymes and microorganisms that are vital 
in the AD processes [16,17]. Most recently, a novel investigation has 
exploited NBW technology for alleviating the inhibitory effect of 
high-salt concentration on methanogenic archaea, such that excellent 
results of 14 %–43 % increase in methane yields and 26 %–58 % increase 
in coenzyme F420 activity have been achieved [12]. As revealed by the 
above-mentioned findings, NBW can serve as an effective strategy for 
addressing the adverse effects of high-salt levels in the AD system. 
Specifically, by utilizing NBW to domesticate AD sludge as inoculum, 
the efficiency of hydrogen production in two-stage AD of FW system 
under salt stress conditions of 20 g NaCl/L can be markedly enhanced, 
and the start-up time of the digester can be substantially shortened [18]. 
Therefore, adopting a strategy that combines NBW with a gradual in­
crease in salinity for domesticating methanogens may represent an 
economical and environmentally friendly approach aimed at optimizing 
the AD efficiency of high-salinity FW. Furthermore, the identification of 
an optimal inoculation ratio (inoculum/substrate (I/S)) in the AD sys­
tem has been heavily investigated since it is a critical parameter that 
exerts a certain effect on the stability of the AD digesters [19,20]. 
However, the optimal I/S ratios for AD of organic solid wastes in the 
adverse environment have been rarely investigated, such that 
high-salinity FW was used in this study.
In this study, the adaptability of inoculum domesticated by NBW in 
the AD of FW was investigated with the increasing salinity levels ranging 
from 1 % to 3 %, to confirm the optimal I/S ratio for AD of the high- 
salinity FW system. First, an acclimatization process was performed by 
ever-increasing salinity from 1 % to 3 %, and the Air-NBW was intro­
duced in the first phase (salinity was 1 %) to domesticate the inoculum. 
The samples that were taken at the end of the respective phase were 
analyzed to determine the electron transport system (ETS) activity, and 
the result can reveal the microbial activity in response to increased 
salinity during the AD of FW with or without the addition of Air-NBW 
domesticated inoculum. Afterward, batch tests were performed at 
varying I/S ratios in the AD of FW under a salinity of 3 % using the 
domesticate inoculum to investigate the effects of inoculation ratios on 
methane production, as well as the concentration of volatile fatty acids 
(VFAs) and alkalinity. This study aimed to provide a long-term stability 
strategy for AD of the high-salinity FW process.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Inoculum, FW, and Air-NBW
In this study, anaerobically digested sludge (AD sludge) was utilized 
as the inoculum and activated under mesophilic conditions (38 ± 1 ◦C) 
for approximately two weeks, until gas production ceased. The initial 
total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) of the inoculum were 2.45 % ±
0.02 % and 1.92 % ± 0.02 %, respectively. A simulated FW with a 
carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio of 18.28, comprising noodles (22 %), rice 
(25 %), pork (16 %), cabbage (29 %), and tofu (8 %), was employed in 
this study, and its TS and VS were determined to be 18.01 % ± 0.01 % 
and 17.59 % ± 0.03 %, respectively. Additionally, the total VFAs con­
centration and pH value were measured as 904.49 ± 24.20 mg/L and 
5.72 ± 0.03, respectively. Consistent with the methodology described in 
Ref. [18], the Air-NBW was manufactured using a gas-water circulation 
method facilitated by an NBW generator. The apparatus was fed with 
both water and air through piping systems, where the flow rates were 
meticulously regulated at 0.05 L/min for the gas and 3 L/min for the 
water. Throughout the entire process, a constant pressure of 0.25 MPa 
was maintained to ensure optimal conditions for the formation of 
nanobubbles. Notably, the air utilized for the generation of Air-NBW was 
sourced directly from the natural environment of the laboratory. The 
Air-NBW with a bubble concentration of (2.9 ± 0.3) × 108 particles/mL 
and a particle size of 38–115 nm was determined after 20 min of 
preparation.
2.2. Acclimatization process by addition of Air-NBW and gradually 
increasing NaCl concentration from 1 % to 3 %
The acclimatization process fell into three phases with the progres­
sively increasing salt concentration. In the first phase, the inoculum was 
domesticated in the AD of FW (salinity of 1 %) system with or without 
Air-NBW introduced, which were termed deionized water (DW) (as the 
control group) and Air-NBW. The experiments were performed in the 
500 mL digesters with the addition of 200 g AD sludge and 10 g FW (wet 
weight) with the I/S ratio (VS basis) of 2 to enrich halotolerant microbial 
consortia by alleviating substrate overload, and the working volume was 
regulated to 350 mL by the DW or Air-NBW. The initial pH reached 6.82 
± 0.09, and not any buffering agents were added to adjust the pH value. 
Subsequently, the NaCl concentration was increased to 2 % and 3 % in 
the second and third phases, respectively. For the above-mentioned two 
phases, there was no re-addition of Air-NBW, but the sludge domesti­
cated by DW or Air-NBW in the first phase served as inoculum. The 
respective digester was fed with the I/S ratio of 2, and the pH reached 
7.27 ± 0.05 and 6.99 ± 0.05 in the second and third phases, respec­
tively. Lastly, the samples were taken at the end of the respective phase 
to analyze the ETS activity.
2.3. Different I/S ratio tests in the AD of FW under a salt level of 3 % by 
using the domesticate inoculum
After the acclimatization process, the I/S ratio continuously declined 
from 2 to 1 and 0.5 for feeding FW to confirm the appropriate I/S for the 
high salinity (3 %) FW AD system. The initial pH of all digesters was 
regulated to 7.5 using 2 M HCl and 2 M NaOH solution. In the above 
process, the samples were regularly taken to determine the variations in 
volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and alkalinity (e.g., the total alkalinity (TA), 
partial alkalinity (PA), as well as intermediate alkalinity (IA)).
For all experiments, the hermetically sealed digesters were purged 
using pure N2 about 3 min, 3 times prior to initiation of the experiments 
to ensure that the anaerobic condition persisted and then operated in an 
incubator with a temperature of 38 ± 1 ◦C.

2.4. Analytical and calculational methods
All liquid samples were first centrifuged to produce the supernatant, 
and then the supernatant was filtrated with a 0.45 μm filter. The stan­
dard methods were adopted to determine the common parameters (e.g., 
TS, VS, TA, PA, and IA) [21]. The concentrations of six common VFAs, 
including acetic acid (HAc), propionic acid (HPr), iso-butyric acid 
(iso-HBu), n-butyric acid (n-HBu), isovaleric acid (iso-HVa), or n-valeric 
acid (n-HVa), were analyzed using a gas chromatograph armed with a 
Unisole F-200 30/60 column and flame ionization detector. In this 
study, the ETS activities were determined by the iodonitrotetrazolium 
dehydrogenase (INT-ETS method) [22]. To be specific, 0.5 mL of sample 
homogenate was taken from the end of the respective phase with a sy­
ringe and injected directly into a 10 mL centrifuge tube. Next, 0.1 mL of 
INT solution (0.2 %, w/v) was introduced. The samples were incubated 
in a 37 ± 1 ◦C table concentrator by shaking at 100 rpm/min for 30 min 
according to the standard, followed by the addition of 1 mL of methanol 
(37 %). After the incubation was terminated, the sample was centrifuged 
at 10,000 r/min for 5 min at 4 ◦C, and the precipitate was introduced 
into 5 mL of methanol. Subsequently, the respective tube was shaken in 
the dark for 10 min at 37 ± 1 ◦C and was centrifuged at 10,000 rpm/min 
for 5 min to take the supernatant to measure absorbance under 485 nm 
(A485). The sediment gained after centrifugation was dried to a constant 
weight in an oven at 105 ◦C, and then the sample was weighed. The 
INT-ETS activity can be determined by Eq. (1) [14]. The pH value was 
monitored using a pH meter (Testo 206, Germany), and all the mea­
surements were performed in triplicate. 
INT-ETS activity = A485⋅V/(KT⋅W⋅T)                                               (1)
where the unit of INT-ETS activity is mg/(g⋅h); A485 denotes absorbance 
under 485 nm; V represents methanol volume; KT expresses the slope of 
the standard curve; W denotes the dry weight of the precipitate; T is 
reaction time (0.5 h).
For the measurement of gas samples, the biogas volumes were 
examined using 20- and 50-mL air-tight syringes at 25 ◦C and 1 atm. 
Subsequently, the contents of CH4 and CO2 were determined using 
another gas chromatograph (GC-8A, Shimadzu, Japan).
2.5. Data processing and statistical analysis
All experiments were performed in duplicate, with each sample 
measured in triplicate. The data were analyzed using Microsoft Office 
Excel 2010 and are presented as mean ± standard deviation. One-way 
analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to determine statistical 
differences among groups using IBM SPSS Statistics, with a p-value 
<0.05 considered statistically significant. All graphical representations 
were prepared using Origin 2019.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. AD performance of the acclimatization process and ETS activity
3.1.1. AD performance of FW with different salinity during the 
acclimatization process
In the first phase, no substantial difference was reported in the daily 
methane production between the DW and Air-NBW digesters (Fig. 1 A), 
and the maximum methane production rate reached 18.22 ± 0.12 and 
21.42 ± 1.15 mL/(g-VSfed⋅d) on 16 days and 18 days in the DW and Air- 
NBW digester at the salinity of 1 %, respectively. Notably, a long start-up 
time of approximately 22 d was identified in the DW group with the 
salinity increased to 2 %, whereas none of this happened in the Air-NBW 
group. As reported by Hou et al. [12], there was a longer start-up period 
(approximately 20 d) when the salt stress was 20 g NaCl/L with or 
without adding Air-NBW in the methanogenesis phase of two-phase AD 
of the FW system with the I/S ratio of 0.5. This indicates that a signifi­
cant reduction in the start-up period of the digesters could be achieved 
by domesticating the inoculum with Air-NBW added and increasing salt 
concentration. This is presumably due to the fact that the domestication 
of microorganisms using Air-NBW enhances their adaptability and 
resilience to stressful conditions such as high salt concentrations. By 
improving mass transfer, enhancing nutrient utilization, promoting 
biological activity, and enabling gradual adaptation, it collectively fa­
cilitates the faster establishment of a functional microbial community, 
thereby significantly reducing the start-up time of AD process.
In addition, the acclimatization process was first operated at the high 
I/S ratio (I/S = 2), such that over-acidification and other undesirable 
phenomena can be avoided effectively. Li et al. [20] demonstrated that 
the acid suppression phenomenon was problematic in the low I/S ratio 
in the AD of FW digesters. For the high-salinity FW, the effects of I/S 
ratios on the methanogenesis performance are discussed in detail in 
section 3.2 of this study. Furthermore, a salt adaptation was obtained 
through a long-term acclimatization process, suggesting that there was 
virtually no lag time in both groups when the salt concentration 
continued to be increased to 3 %. The peak values of daily methane 
production in this phase were elevated to 22.11 ± 0.12 and 26.021 ±
2.21 mL/(g-VSfed⋅d) with or without the addition of the Air-NBW, 
respectively.
Multitudinous studies proved that high-salt concentration could 
dramatically influence AD performance. For instance, Zhao et al. [23] 
reported that the maximum methane yield was only 22.7 mL/g-VSfed in 
the one-phase FW AD digester with the 15.0 g NaCl/L. Liu et al. [24] also 
found that the methane yield in the one-phase AD of kitchen waste was 
decreased from 311.9 to 133.6 mL/g-VSfed when the salt concentration 
was increased from 0 to 25 g NaCl/L. In contrast, the cumulative CH4 
yields in both groups were increased rather than decreased with the 
increase of the salinity from 1 % to 3 % in this study (Fig. 1 B). To be 
more specific, the final cumulative methane yield was improved from 
122.15 ± 0.63 to 173.21 ± 9.14 mL/g-VSfed in the DW group (p = 0.005 
< 0.05) and from 160.13 ± 8.67 to 201.02 ± 0.53 mL/g-VSfed (p =
0.044 < 0.05). As expected, all cumulative methane yields in the 
Air-NBW digesters were more efficient than those in the DW digesters in 
the three phases, marking an increase of 31 %, 18 %, and 16 %, 
respectively, and semblable conclusions were reported by Chen et al. 
[25].
Furthermore, Wang et al. [15] have discovered that O2-NBW dem­
onstrates remarkable effectiveness in facilitating transmembrane trans­
port of organic substances, which might accelerate the growth process of 
methanogenic microorganisms. The micro-oxygen environment created 
by O2-NBW positively stimulates the synthesis of ATP, enabling more 
efficient metabolic activities and providing sufficient energy support for 
cellular processes such as metabolism, growth, and signal transduction. 
In high-salinity environments, the cellular membranes of microorgan­
isms may be damaged, affecting the efficiency of substance transport, 
and frequently, their energy metabolism is severely impacted, leading to 
decreased growth rates and slowed metabolic activities. However, NBW 
could assist in improving the efficiency of substance transport for mi­
croorganisms under high-salinity conditions, stimulating more efficient 
metabolic activities, and thereby mitigating the inhibitory effects of high 
salinity to a certain extent.
3.1.2. ETS activity
Microbial activity is capable of largely regulating the outcome of 
methane production in AD systems, especially in the presence of unde­
sirable factors. To a certain extent, ETS activity reveals the adaption of 
microorganisms in the AD system at high salinity, and Fig. 2 presents the 
results of ETS activity at the end of the respective phase, consistent with 
the results of methanogenesis performance. Moreover, the ETS activity 
was increased from 25.10 ± 4.69 and 35.98 ± 5.06 mg/(g⋅h) to 68.69 ±
8.28 and 87.03 ± 10.03 mg/(g⋅h) in the DW and Air-NBW digesters at 
the salinity elevated from 1 % to 3 %, respectively. The experimental 
data demonstrate that acclimating microbial inoculum through Air- 
NBW introduction during the initial phase could significantly en­
hances enzymatic activity (particularly ETS activity) in AD systems 
under hypersaline stress. This metabolic stimulation likely explains the 
superior methane production observed in Air-NBW reactors compared to 
conventional acclimation approaches.
As revealed by the above-mentioned results, using the inoculum 
domesticate through the introduction of Air-NBW in the first phase and 
increasing salt concentration can lead to the significantly enhanced 
tolerance of microorganisms under the high-salt concentration in the AD 
digester. Compared with our existing research, this strategy may be 
more effective in obtaining higher methane production. Another study 
by Chen et al. [25] has suggested that the improvement of microbial 
adaptations by the gradually increased salt concentration leads to the 
increased abundance ratio of halotolerant microbes, as confirmed by an 
enhancement in their hydrolytic and acidogenic abilities with the in­
cremental increase in salinity. Furthermore, Zhang et al. [10] confirmed 
that the abundance ratios of Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina are 
elevated from 16.46 % and 8.77 % to 22.08 % and 10.01 %, respectively 
after acclimatization with the rise of the NaCl concentration in the AD of 
kitchen waste. Likewise, Wang et al. [26] indicated that Methanolinea, 
Methanospirillum, and Methanoculleus exhibit varying degrees of adap­
tation to salinity. Building on these findings, Air-NBW technology could 
activate microbial metabolic pathways and associated enzymatic cas­
cades. Complementarily, the phased salinity acclimatization protocol 
employs incremental ionic strength adjustments, enabling strategic mi­
crobial community succession toward halotolerant phenotypes. There­
fore, the integrated strategy of Air-NBW application with progressive

salinity acclimation exhibits potential in significantly reducing the

3.2. Effects of inoculum ratio on methanogenesis performance from the 
FW AD system under a salt level of 3 % using the domesticate inoculum
3.2.1. Methanogenesis performance
The I/S ratio has always been considered a vital parameter affecting 
the efficiency and stability of AD [27]. Although the effects of different 
I/S ratios on AD performance have been extensively investigated, their 
effects on AD of organic solid wastes in adverse environments (such as 
high salinity) have scarcely been investigated. In this study, the effects of 
different I/S ratios on methanogenesis performance in the AD of FW 
under a salt level of 3 % were investigated using the domesticated 
inoculum, and the relevant results are presented in Fig. 3. Besides, the 
I/S ratio declined from 2 to 1, and the operating cycle (around 30 d) 
remained largely unchanged (Fig. 3 A). However, the peak values of 
28.61 ± 3.40 and 30.91 ± 0.17 mL/(g-VSfed⋅d) at the I/S ratio of 1 were 
identified on 12 and 10 d in the DW and Air-NBW digesters, respectively, 
appearing earlier than the peak values at the I/S ratio of 2 (on 18 days in 
both groups).
In contrast, as the I/S ratio declined from 2 to 0.5, the AD digesters 
were operated approximately for 70 d till almost no biogas production 
was detected. The Gompertz model was selected to resolve lag-phase 
dynamics in methane production, as it explicitly parameterizes micro­
bial lag time (λ) under inhibitory conditions. Kinetic analysis revealed 
that the λ was lengthened with the decline of the I/S ratio, particularly in 
the DW group (Table 1). To be specific, the λ was extended 2 times in the 
DW group with the decline of the I/S ratio from 2 to 0.5. As revealed by 
the above results, the high I/S ratio can lead to the shortened operating 
period of digesters and the improved methane production rate by sup­
plying more methanogenic bacteria, and other research has drawn 
similar conclusions [28].
Fig. 3 B illustrates the corresponding cumulative methane yield in 
the DW and Air-NBW groups with the different I/S ratios. The cumula­
tive methane yield in the DW groups reached 199.33 ± 9.92 and 262.93 
± 3.69 mL/g-VSfed at I/S ratios of 1 and 0.5, respectively, representing 
increases of approximately 15 % and 52 % compared to the DW group 
with an I/S ratio of 2. Compared to the DW groups at equivalent I/S 
ratios, the Air-NBW digester showed a non-significant increase to 228.88 
± 4.36 mL/g-VSfed at an I/S ratio of 1 (p = 0.061) but achieved a sta­
tistically significant higher yield of 307.45 ± 3.77 mL/g-VSfed at an I/S 
ratio of 0.5 (p = 0.007 < 0.05). The above results were not consistent 
with the findings of other studies where the higher methane yield is 
achieved in the digesters with the high I/S ratio [29,30]. The inconsis­
tency in results may be clarified by differences in the activity of the 
inoculated microorganisms. As discussed in the research of Elbeshbishy 
et al. [31], the ability to produce methane could be increased under low

I/S ratios if sufficient nutrients are supplied. Moreover, Kong et al. [32] 
suggested a higher methane yield at the minimum I/S ratio of 0.25 when 
inoculating pre-incubated inoculum. In contrast, more inoculum (high 
I/S ratio) should be provided to metabolize the substrate for respect to 
non-incubated inoculum with low microbial activity. Besides, Xing et al. 
[33] confirmed that the cumulative methane production declines 
decreased the decrease of I/S for the seed sludge without domesticating, 
whereas the long-term acclimatization of inoculum will change the 
optimal I/S ratio. In this study, the inoculum was domesticated by 
Air-NBW, and the gradual increase of the NaCl concentration, such that 
the sample exhibited high microbial activity and high methane yield. 
From the perspective of methane production and running time, the I/S 
ratio of 1 was confirmed to be optimal for AD of FW exhibiting high 
salinity.
3.2.2. Variations in pH, VFAs, and alkalinity
The pH of the inoculum reached 6.76 ± 0.08 and 6.88 ± 0.03 in the 
control and Air-NBW digesters, respectively, when the acclimatization 
process was completed. The original pH of all digesters was fitted to 7.5 
in the experiment of this study using 2 M HCl and/or 2 M NaOH solution. 
As depicted in Fig. 4, the pH fluctuations of all digesters displayed 
similar trends in the AD process. On that basis, the pH value was first 
decreased and then increased, and the decrease rate of the pH value was 
elevated with the reduction of the I/S ratio. Existing research has 
generally suggested that lower I/S ratios can lead to lower pH values 
[34], and this finding was also indicated by the result of this study. The 
minimum pH values in the DW and Air-NBW groups reached 5.93 ±
0.01 and 6.16 ± 0.01 at the I/S ratio of 1 and 5.25 ± 0.00 and 5.39 ±
0.01 at the I/S ratio of 0.5 on 6 d. Moreover, the pH value was recovered 
to nearly 7.00 (favorable for methanogenesis) on 12 days and 30 days at 
the I/S ratio of 1 and 0.5, respectively. When the experiment was about 
to end, the pH values in the DW and Air-NBW groups reached 8.30 ±
0.09 and 8.33 ± 0.02 at the I/S ratio of 1 and 7.49 ± 0.01 and 7.78 ±
0.00 at the I/S ratio of 0.5.
Fig. 4 also presents the changes in TA, such that the pH can always be 
kept in the ideal range (6.8–7.8) to avoid the accumulation of VFAs in 
the AD system [35]. At the I/S ratio of 1, the TA continued to increase, 
whereas the TA was decreased first and then increased in the digesters at 
the I/S ratio of 0.5. As revealed by the above-mentioned results, low I/S 
ratios may result in the acidification of the AD digesters, such that 
methane production can be inhibited, especially in the DW group. In 
other words, the microorganisms domesticated by Air-NBW turned out 
to exhibit more resistance to the adverse environment of the system after 
a long period of salt acclimatization. Furthermore, with the rise in TA, 
the pH value of all digesters was recovered, and the methanogens can be 
activated to produce more methane.
The results of pH values corresponded to the variations in VFAs 
concentration, and the distribution of VFAs from different pathways in 
the AD process can more significantly indicate the health of AD (e.g., the 
acidogenesis balance and methanogenesis balance) [36]. Fig. 5 A and B 
describe the impact of the I/S ratio on VFAs compositions during the AD 
of FW at the salinity of 3 %. To be specific, the concentration of total 
VFAs was steadily elevated in all digesters; subsequently, it declined 
significantly in the digesters at the I/S ratio of 1 but decreased slowly in 
the digesters with the I/S ratio of 0.5. The maximum concentrations of 
total VFAs reached 3438.61 ± 53.34 and 3284.36 ± 67.20 mg/L in the 
control and Air-NBW digesters at the I/S ratio of 1 and 5908.96 ± 41.05 
and 6413.28 ± 65.49 mg/L in the control and Air-NBW digesters at the 
I/S ratio of 0.5, respectively.
The above results may explain why the lag time was longer at the I/S 
ratio of 0.5, primarily due to the accumulation of VFAs that can lead to 
the generation of an acidic environment. Thus, methane production will 
be hindered. For the individual VFA concentration, acetic acid (HAc), 
and butyric acid predominated in the acid accumulation phase, ac­
counting for nearly 90 % and 88 % at the I/S ratio of 1 and 0.5. Existing 
research has suggested that HAc is considered a preferable substrate for 
CH4 production, such that the high concentration of substrate with the 
higher methane yield is likely to be explained.
3.2.3. Process stability
The alkalinity and VFAs are considered a buffering combination in 
AD reactions, and VFA/TA and IA/PA ratios always serve as the greater 
parameters that are capable of monitoring the stability of the AD system. 
Fig. 6 presents the profiles of IA/PA ratio and VFA/TA ratio from the FW 
AD system at the salinity of 3 % using the domesticated inoculum. The 
IA/PA ratio in the digesters with the I/S ratio of 1 declined steadily from 
the maximum value (3.61 ± 0.24 in the DW group and 2.51 ± 0.26 in 
the Air-NBW group) on 6 d to 0.60 ± 0.02 in the DW group and 0.28 ±
0.01 in the Air-NBW group at the end of process, respectively. As 
revealed by the above result, the digesters at the I/S ratio of 1 exhibited 
better stability than the digesters at the I/S ratio of 0.5. It is noteworthy 
that the IA/PA ratio fluctuated considerably in digesters at the I/S of 0.5 
in the prophase of the reaction. The above result suggested an extremely 
unstable system since an abrupt rise in the IA/PA ratio commonly rep­
resents a fall in pH buffering ability [16].
Besides, the results of the VFA/TA ratio indicated the process sta­
bility. The VFA/TA ratio of digesters with the I/S ratio of 1 dramatically 
declined, which was lower than 0.4 on 6 days, suggesting that the system 
regained stability. However, the instability persisted for a long time in 
the digesters with the I/S of 0.5 in accordance with the higher VFA/TA 
ratio. The reason for the above result is that the AD process is optimally 
stable at IA/PA ratio below 0.4, and the digester is prone to significant 
instability at IA/PA ratio above 0.8, as confirmed by a previous study 
[37]. Furthermore, the stability of the Air-NBW system was superior to 
that of the DW system regardless of the I/S ratio.
4. Conclusions
Domestication with Air-NBW significantly reduces start-up time and 
enhances methane yields in high-salinity digesters. Moreover, the
